title: Why every AI-made game in Godot starts out looking the same
author: flockbaygames
selftext:
gave Opus 5.5 in Claude Code four one-line prompts, a 3D platformer, a top-down shooter, a 3D racer and a small island to explore, each in an empty folder with nothing else. the code was honestly fine, it added coyote time, a jump buffer, screen shake and a dash nobody asked for

but there wasn't one image, sound or font in any of the four folders, so everything fell back to engine defaults. capsule hero, circle enemies, cone trees, the built-in font and nearly the same blue sky in all three 3D games

second pass I gave each one free art, sounds and a font and asked it to pick a palette, a sky and a time of day. 3 of 4 went golden hour and 3 built their menus from the same cream, gold and coral, so asking it to choose just gets you a new default. takeaway is name the choice yourself instead of asking it to pick

what default do you see most in AI-made games?

comments.author: WhosLive
comments.body: That matches what a lot of people see. Models usually fall back to the most common choice whenever you leave a slot open, so the defaults repeat. Worth trying a short style sheet up front with the palette hex codes, the time of day, the font and a couple of reference games, so it never has to pick. Even swapping one or two of those per project tends to break the sameness fast.

comments.author: katatonicmango
comments.body: Awesome video! Great insight. I look forward to seeing more videos from your channel!

comments.author: max13007
comments.body:
Facts. Just today I was working on a platforming section on a game I'm working on. There's a moving platform that you need to hop on and off of in order to correctly navigate the scene. And at one point, you can miss the platform and become stranded. 

Claude automatically built in a feature that would make the platform return to the start if it hit the end of the level without you on it. Which... yes, that does "solve" the issue. But it making that choice robbed me of having a more complex, interesting or unique way to fix that issue. 

I implemented a rule for this and all future games (paraphrasing): let me know when a player might get stuck, and you're free to make suggestions, but do not build a solution I did not ask for.

I'm hundreds of hours into dev with AI, and it's becoming more and more clear to me just how many choices the AI makes for you that normally would need to be my decisions during the design process. It's in those details sometimes that a game becomes its own thing vs just copying an existing product. 

I will likely need to rebuild some of my earlier prototypes because they are so filled with choices I didn't make, that I may as well start from scratch.

replies.author: flockbaygames
replies.body: yeah the platform thing is exactly it. in my test it put coyote time, a jump buffer and a dash into one line prompts that never asked for any of it. fine code but those were design calls it made for me. is your rule in `CLAUDE.md` or do you paste it in each session?

replies.author: max13007
replies.body: I've got a folder for markdown rules, so each projects has its own set of rules, and there's a primary CLAUDE.md that is referenced first. This rule went into the general md

replies.author: Arya_the_Gamer
replies.body: A better solution is to use lower reasoning levels like on low thinking instead of high or max. Or just turn off reasoning entirely if possible but then it won't be able to account for edge cases.

comments.author: Arya_the_Gamer
comments.body:
Umm no shit, that's how I usually start with when prototyping stuff in just about any engine(pre ai): capsule as a player, prototype grid textures and most placeholder stuff ranges from being cubes to cylinders or a combination of both.

You shouldn't care about defaults during early stages where you're prototyping stuff. Once the mechanical framework is done, get to work on the visual assets. Atleast that's how I approach projects.

comments.body: Don't let the model make design choices it sucks
